section.heading: 7.7 Solving Systems with Inverses
Learning Objectives

list.item: Find the inverse of a matrix.
Solve a system of linear equations using an inverse matrix.

section.paragraph: Soriya plans to invest \$10,500 into two different bonds to spread out her risk. The first bond has an annual return of 10%, and the second bond has an annual return of 6%. In order to receive an 8.5% return from the two bonds, how much should Soriya invest in each bond? What is the best method to solve this problem?

There are several ways we can solve this problem. As we have seen in previous sections, systems of equations and matrices are useful in solving real-world problems involving finance. After studying this section, we will have the tools to solve the bond problem using the inverse of a matrix.
section.heading: Finding the Inverse of a Matrix
section.paragraph: We know that the multiplicative inverse of a real number $$a$$ is $$a^{-1},$$ and $$aa^{-1} = a^{-1}a = \left( \frac{1}{a} \right)a = 1.$$ For example, $$2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$$ and $$\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)2 = 1.$$ The multiplicative inverse of a matrix is similar in concept, except that the product of matrix $$A$$ and its inverse $$A^{-1}$$ equals the identity matrix. The identity matrix is a square matrix containing ones down the main diagonal and zeros everywhere else. We identify identity matrices by $$I_{n}$$ where $$n$$ represents the dimension of the matrix. Observe the following equations.
$$I_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$
$$I_{3} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrrrr} 1 & & 0 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 1 & & 0 \\ 0 & & 0 & & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$
The identity matrix acts as a 1 in matrix algebra. For example, $$AI = IA = A.$$
A matrix that has a multiplicative inverse has the properties
$$\begin{array}{l} {AA^{-1} = I} \\ {A^{-1}A = I} \end{array}$$

A matrix that has a multiplicative inverse is called an invertible matrix. Only a square matrix may have a multiplicative inverse, as the reversibility, $$AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I,$$ is a requirement. Not all square matrices have an inverse, but if $$A$$ is invertible, then $$A^{-1}$$ is unique. We will look at two methods for finding the inverse of a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix and a third method that can be used on both $$2 \times 2$$ and $$3 \times 3$$ matrices.

section.heading: Finding the Multiplicative Inverse Using Matrix Multiplication
section.paragraph: We can now determine whether two matrices are inverses, but how would we find the inverse of a given matrix? Since we know that the product of a matrix and its inverse is the identity matrix, we can find the inverse of a matrix by setting up an equation using matrix multiplication.

example.title: Finding the Multiplicative Inverse Using Matrix Multiplication

problem.paragraph: Use matrix multiplication to find the inverse of the given matrix.

solution.paragraph: For this method, we multiply $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & & 4 \\ -1 & & -3 \end{array} \right\rbrack,B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} -3 & & -4 \\ 1 & & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ by a matrix containing unknown constants and set it equal to the identity.
Find the product of the two matrices on the left side of the equal sign.

Next, set up a system of equations with the entry in row 1, column 1 of the new matrix equal to the first entry of the identity, 1. Set the entry in row 2, column 1 of the new matrix equal to the corresponding entry of the identity, which is 0.

Using row operations, multiply and add as follows: $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {1a-2c} & {1b-2d} \\ {2a-3c} & {2b-3d} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ Add the equations, and solve for $$\begin{matrix} {1a-2c = 1R_{1}} \\ {2a-3c = 0R_{2}} \end{matrix}$$

Write another system of equations setting the entry in row 1, column 2 of the new matrix equal to the corresponding entry of the identity, 0. Set the entry in row 2, column 2 equal to the corresponding entry of the identity.

Using row operations, multiply and add as follows: $$\begin{array}{r} {a-2(-2) = 1} \\ {a + 4 = 1} \\ {a = -3} \end{array}$$ Add the two equations and solve for $$\begin{array}{rr} {1b-2d = 0} & R_{1} \\ {2b-3d = 1} & R_{2} \end{array}$$
Once more, back-substitute and solve for $$d.$$

section.heading: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using the Inverse of a Matrix
section.paragraph: Solving a system of linear equations using the inverse of a matrix requires the definition of two new matrices: $$\end{array} {AA^{-1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \end{array} { = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} {2(-1) + 3(-1) + 1(6)} & { 2(1) + 3(0) + 1(-2)} & { 2(0) + 3(1) + 1(-3)} \\ {3(-1) + 3(-1) + 1(6)} & { 3(1) + 3(0) + 1(-2)} & { 3(0) + 3(1) + 1(-3)} \\ {2(-1) + 4(-1) + 1(6)} & { 2(1) + 4(0) + 1(-2)} & { 2(0) + 4(1) + 1(-3)} \end{array} \right\rbrack} { = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \end{array}\]$$ is the matrix representing the variables of the system, and $$\[\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \\$$ is the matrix representing the constants. Then $$AX = B.$$ looks like
$$\begin{matrix} {a_{1}x + b_{1}y = c_{1}} \\ {a_{2}x + b_{2}y = c_{2}} \end{matrix}$$

Recall the discussion earlier in this section regarding multiplying a real number by its inverse, $$A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{1} & b_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ To solve a single linear equation $$X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}$$ for $$B = \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$ we would simply multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of $$AX = B$$ Thus,
$$\begin{bmatrix} a_{1} & b_{1} \\ a_{2} & b_{2} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{bmatrix}$$

The only difference between a solving a linear equation and a system of equations written in matrix form is that finding the inverse of a matrix is more complicated, and matrix multiplication is a longer process. However, the goal is the same—to isolate the variable.
We will investigate this idea in detail, but it is helpful to begin with a $$(2^{-1}) 2 = \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) 2 = 1.$$ system and then move on to a $$ax = b$$ system.

note.title: Q&A
note.paragraph: If the coefficient matrix does not have an inverse, does that mean the system has no solution?
No, if the coefficient matrix is not invertible, the system could be inconsistent and have no solution, or be dependent and have infinitely many solutions.

example.title: Solving a 2 × 2 System Using the Inverse of a Matrix

problem.paragraph: Solve the given system of equations using the inverse of a matrix.

solution.paragraph: Write the system in terms of a coefficient matrix, a variable matrix, and a constant matrix.
First, we need to calculate $$A$$ Using the formula to calculate the inverse of a 2 by 2 matrix, we have:

$$\begin{array}{r} {\left( A^{-1} \right)AX = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {\left\lbrack {\left( A^{-1} \right)A} \right\rbrack X = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {IX = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \\ {X = \left( A^{-1} \right)B} \end{array}$$

Now we are ready to solve. Multiply both sides of the equation by $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 11 \end{bmatrix},X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix},B = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}$$

note.title: Q&A
note.paragraph: Can we solve for $$\begin{array}{l} {A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} d & {- b} \\ {- c} & a \end{array} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{1}{3(11)-8(4)}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 11 & -8 \\ -4 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \\ { = \frac{1}{1}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 11 & -8 \\ -4 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$ by finding the product $$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & -8 \\ -4 & { 3} \end{bmatrix}$$
No, recall that matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $$A^{-1}.$$ Consider our steps for solving the matrix equation.

$$\begin{array}{l} {(A^{-1})AX = (A^{-1})B} \\ {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 11 & -8 \\ -4 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 11 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 11 & -8 \\ -4 & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} 5 \\ 7 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \\ {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {11(5) + (-8)7} \\ {-4(5) + 3(7)} \end{array} \right\rbrack} \\ {\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} x \\ y \end{array} \right\rbrack = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} -1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$

Notice in the first step we multiplied both sides of the equation by $$\left( {-1,1} \right).$$ but the $$X$$ was to the left of $$BA^{-1}?$$ on the left side and to the left of $$A^{-1}B \neq BA^{-1}.$$ on the right side. Because matrix multiplication is not commutative, order matters.
